enrichment.short_title: Attorney General obtains unlimited civil proceedings order against habitual vexatious litigant Anthony Alexander
key_facts: The Attorney General applied under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981 for a civil proceedings order against Anthony Alexander, an unqualified person who had acted in litigation for others and in his own name.

Between 1997 and 2002 Mr Alexander featured in ten cases involving banks, Halifax, Phillips Electronics, bankruptcy, possession and related appeals; 49 separate applications and appeals were identified, all ultimately unsuccessful.

Three civil restraint (formerly Grepe v Loam) orders had already been made against him, including after the Court of Appeal in Noueiri v Paragon Finance restrained him from acting for others in the Royal Courts of Justice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's application to the Administrative Court for a section 42 civil proceedings order; permission to appeal refused at the end of the hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Civil proceedings order granted without time limit; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A person who habitually and persistently makes vexatious applications in civil proceedings, including repeated permission-to-appeal applications to the Court of Appeal, may be made subject to a section 42 civil proceedings order; section 42(1)(b) extends to vexatious applications in civil proceedings whether instituted by the applicant or another, and the court may rely on findings in underlying proceedings when exercising its discretion.

Whether habitual and persistent vexatious conduct is established where most litigation activity was as defendant rather than claimant
What legal principles govern the exercise of discretion under section 42
Whether the defendant's litigation history satisfies the tests of habituality, persistence and absence of reasonable ground

enrichment.short_title: CIPLA alendronate process held not to infringe Merck patent after strict claim construction
key_facts: Merck sued Generics (UK) Ltd for infringement of EP (UK) 0,402,152, a process patent for making monosodium alendronate using methanesulfonic acid (MSA) to keep the reaction fluid and homogeneous.
Generics intended to import alendronate made in India by CIPLA using a confidential process that did not use MSA and differed materially on pH adjustment, crystallisation and washing steps.
Validity was not tried; the parties agreed the only issue was construction of claim 1, yet the trial ran four days at combined costs exceeding £850,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Patents Court speedy trial on infringement only; validity counterclaim stayed.
enrichment.outcome: No infringement; CIPLA process held outside the scope of claim 1 whether by direct Protocol/Catnic construction or by application of the Improver questions.
enrichment.ratio: Patent monopoly must be discernible from the claims without experiments; the Protocol requires protection only for embodiments the skilled reader would conclude with reasonable confidence the patentee intended to cover, and fairness does not permit extending protection to variants the patentee expressly limited or did not intend to include, including other sulphonic acids for MSA and alternative work-up steps in stages (c) to (e) of claim 1.
legal_issues: Whether the CIPLA process infringed claim 1 by equivalence despite omitting MSA and four of five specified process stages
How Article 69 EPC and the Protocol govern purposive construction of chemical process claims
Whether the Improver questions or experiments are appropriate where claim language is clear
Whether replacing MSA with another liquid sulphonic acid works in the same way to achieve the patented high purity and 85–90% yield

enrichment.short_title: Widower's clinical negligence appeal dismissed where GP delay did not cause wife's fatal pulmonary embolism
key_facts: Peter Wardlaw sued Dr Farrar after his wife died aged 69 from massive bilateral pulmonary emboli following delayed hospital admission.
On 14 September 1997 Dr Farrar was found negligent in failing to consider pulmonary embolism and arrange admission; she was not admitted until 21 September.

The trial judge found the week's delay caused pain and suffering but did not materially contribute to death; Mrs Wardlaw later deteriorated despite heparin and warfarin, fitting Dr Hill's category of patients who do not respond to anticoagulation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against Manchester County Court award of £1,000 damages for clinical negligence.
enrichment.ratio: Where a trial judge prefers one expert's clinical evidence over another on causation and finds that a delay in treatment did not increase the risk of death, the Court of Appeal will not interfere; later failure of anticoagulant therapy may properly be taken into account when assessing whether earlier admission would have changed the outcome, and statistical evidence such as the ICOPER registry cannot safely predict individual outcomes without agreed definitions of haemodynamic instability.
legal_issues: Whether the seven-day delay in hospital admission caused Mrs Wardlaw's death
Whether the ICOPER pulmonary embolism registry statistics could establish causation
Whether a growing thrombus between 14 and 21 September made death more probable
Whether Hotson v Berkshire Area Health Authority required assessment of probabilities only as at 14 September
Whether fresh textbook evidence should be admitted on appeal

statutes_considered.title: European Convention for the Protection of Animals Kept for Farming Purposes

enrichment.short_title: Skipper acquitted where entering fisheries zone to break nets on rocks held not a fishing operation

statutes_considered.title: South Wales Sea Fisheries Committee Byelaws

key_facts: Beam trawler Admiral Blake, skippered by Malcolm Saunders and owned by IF Ltd, entered the South Wales Sea Fisheries Committee six-mile limit on 19 July 2002 with nets in the water.

The vessel exceeded the 150 vessel capacity unit limit and lacked a boat fishing permit; Saunders deliberately entered the limit to break open nets on rocks to release debris, rocks and fish, then streamed and hauled the nets.
Magistrates found no fishing was undertaken within the six-mile area and acquitted the defendants; the committee appealed by case stated against Saunders only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Prosecutor's appeal by case stated to the Divisional Court from magistrates' acquittal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; case stated question answered in favour of the respondent.
enrichment.ratio: Entering a sea fisheries district to break nets on the seabed and release debris and fish, or to stream nets free of sand, is not using a method or instrument of fishing nor using a boat in a fishing operation within the meaning of byelaws 38 and 41; where statutory wording is ambiguous in a penal context it must be resolved in the defendant's favour.

Whether nets lowered in an open state to stream debris constitute using an instrument of fishing

enrichment.short_title: ATCSA detainees fail to overturn tape-recorded monitoring of media interviews
key_facts: Six foreign nationals certified under section 21 ATCSA 2001 and detained in high-security prisons sought judicial review of the Home Secretary's refusal to allow unmonitored media interviews.

Claimants feared misinterpretation of statements, repercussions from prison staff, and transmission of confidential information to allied repressive regimes.

enrichment.ratio: Monitoring conditions requiring interviews with suspected terrorist detainees to be conducted within earshot of officials and tape-recorded are a proportionate restriction on Article 10(1) freedom of expression where they serve legitimate aims of prison discipline and national security under Article 10(2), especially for category A prisoners certified under ATCSA; courts defer to executive judgment on national security while reviewing lawfulness.

Whether ATCSA detainees should be treated differently from convicted prisoners for media access purposes

enrichment.short_title: Hagans and Wilson convictions quashed after discredited West Midlands Serious Crime Squad evidence
key_facts: Christopher Hagans and John Wilson were convicted at Leicester Crown Court in 1983 of conspiracy to rob and related offences arising from a series of linked trials.

Prosecution relied heavily on supergrass Richard Mackay and oral confessions attributed by West Midlands Police Serious Crime Squad officers, all of whom were later discredited and the squad disbanded in 1989.
McKinnon J found in civil proceedings that officers including those who interviewed Hagans assaulted Derek Treadaway and gave false evidence; the Crown did not seek to uphold either conviction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Linked appeals referred by the Criminal Cases Review Commission under section 9 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1995; appeals unopposed.
enrichment.ratio: Convictions cannot be regarded as safe where the most important prosecution evidence comes from a supergrass handled by discredited Serious Crime Squad officers whose evidence has led to multiple quashed convictions and whose dishonesty has been judicially established.
legal_issues: Whether convictions based on Mackay and SCS officer evidence remain safe after discreditation of the squad
Whether separate supporting evidence saves a conviction where core prosecution evidence is tainted
Effect of McKinnon J's civil findings on the officers' credibility

enrichment.short_title: Landlord denied section 12 extension after missing one-month rent review arbitration deadline post-Starmark
key_facts: Claimants acquired the freehold of premises let to Pizza Express under a 1997 lease with quinquennial upward-only rent reviews and clause 8.2(E) deeming tenant-proposed rent agreed unless landlord applies for RICS appointment within one month.

After Starmark Enterprises Ltd v CPL Distribution Ltd [2002] held time of the essence for such clauses, tenant served notice proposing £21,000 on review date 30 October 2002; claimants' RICS application was late.
Claimants sought extension under section 12(3)(a) arguing the Starmark change in law was outside parties' contemplation when the lease was made in October 1997.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court claim for order extending time to apply for arbitrator appointment under section 12 Arbitration Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; court held no jurisdiction to extend time.
enrichment.ratio: A change in Court of Appeal authority on whether time is of the essence in rent review clauses does not satisfy section 12(3)(a) because legal change was foreseeable, did not cause the failure to comply with the contractual time bar, and parties must be assumed to have contemplated ordinary commercial omissions by advisers; Harbour v Environment Agency governs the restrictive approach to extending contractual time bars.
legal_issues: Whether clause 8.2(E) is a time bar within section 12(1) Arbitration Act 1996
Whether the Starmark decision was a circumstance outside reasonable contemplation of the parties
Whether change in law caused or contributed to failure to apply for arbitrator within one month
Whether it would be just to extend time if the first condition were satisfied

enrichment.short_title: Four-year total sentence upheld for serial burglar including maximum Bail Act term
key_facts: Appellant pleaded guilty to two dwelling burglaries committed on bail, theft of books, and failing to surrender to bail after missing a magistrates' hearing.
He had 21 prior burglaries or attempted thefts from dwellings and a manslaughter conviction arising from an earlier burglary; eight further offences were taken into consideration.
Crown Court imposed 42 months concurrent on burglaries, three months consecutive for theft, and three months consecutive for bail breach, totalling four years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to Court of Appeal against sentence; leave granted if required on Bail Act count.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; four-year total sentence unchanged.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant is committed to the Crown Court under section 6 of the Powers of Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act rather than section 6(6) Bail Act for inadequacy of magistrates' powers, the maximum sentence for a section 6(1) Bail Act offence remains three months unless treated as contempt; even at the maximum, a consecutive bail sentence may stand where totality requires a long-term prisoner sentence reflecting overall criminality.

Whether Crown Court had power to impose more than three months for the bail offence on this committal route
Whether three months at maximum without discount was manifestly excessive
